newsitem.title: CHINA: HK stocks slide sharply in late trade, close down.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks slide sharply in late trade, close down.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks closed sharply lower on Friday after a last-minute slide led by HSBC and compounded by a weak property sector, and brokers said they expected to see the market consolidate further on Monday.
"There's a rumour that one of the big brokers has downgraded Hongkong Bank," said Priscilla Cheung, dealing director at Dao Heng Securities. "But it looks to me like profit-taking only."
The Hang Seng Index slid from positive territory in the last 20 minutes of trade to end 135.89 points, or 0.87 percent, lower at 15,570.40. The blue-chip index had hit a high of 15,769.35.
Turnover eased to a healthy HK$20.82 billion from Thursday's HK$22.83 billion.
"The market was very volatile," said a broker with a large British house. "HSBC was through the floor and Hongkong Telecom through the roof."
HSBC and Hongkong Telecom -- two of the largest blue chips -- dominated trading, followed by selected H shares.
"The bear squeeze on HSBC may be over," said the British broker.
HSBC, which leaped HK$15.00 on Thursday, closed HK$14.00 lower at HK$265.00 on heavy trade of HK$2.04 billion.
Hongkong Telecom surged to an all-time high of HK$20.40 before ending HK$1.05 higher at HK$20.15, a record close. Turnover was HK$1.49 billion.
Brokers said the heavy volume and strong buying interest in the share pointed to derivatives' issuers buying in advance of the issue of a new product.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see several covered warrants on Hongkong Telecom come out later today," said Janet Gillies, sales director at OCBC Securities.
Trading in red chips and selected H-shares remained brisk.

The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index for H-shares slipped 4.66 points, or 0.40 percent, to 1,147.01, while the Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index for red chips gained 3.78 points, or 0.11 percent to 3,387.48.
H-share Shanghai Haixin was one of the most actively traded shares on rumours of plans for a red-chip style restructuring, brokers said. The share closed HK$0.35 higher at HK$5.50.
Second-line red chip CNPC (Hong Kong) eased HK$0.075 to HK$2.30, while Poly Investment leaped HK$0.19 to HK$1.74.
"These issues are very much sentiment-driven," said the U.K. broker.
The property sector inched down, led by Cheung Kong's HK$1.00 fall to HK$74.50.
